messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran was 54 when she came to treatment, a divorced Vietnamese American woman who had spent most of her adult life working as an electrician, proud of being steady-handed and practical in job sites where she was often the only woman. The event she returned to in the first sessions was not an accident at work but a life-threatening illness that had unfolded in a hospital room two years earlier. She described waking one night unable to draw a full breath, hearing the harsh, laboring sound of her own breathing fill the room while staff moved quickly around her bed. What stayed with her most vividly was the sterile bite of antiseptic in the air and the animal panic of listening to herself fight for oxygen, certain for several minutes that she was about to die. Even now, when she talked about it, she seemed to brace in her chair as if her body were remembering before she had finished the sentence.

In the months after she was discharged, those sensory details began to appear in ordinary life with an intensity that surprised her. The smell of disinfectant in a clinic hallway, a whiff of antiseptic cleaner in a grocery store restroom, or hearing someone nearby breathe heavily could stop her cold. At work, if she was in a cramped utility room with a coworker exerting himself and breathing hard, her chest would tighten and her body would go rigid before she could tell herself where she really was. Around the anniversary of the hospitalization, she became especially watchful and short-tempered, already tense from the moment she woke. She said her body seemed to “jump first and ask questions later,” with pounding heart, tight muscles, and a sense of danger arriving ahead of thought.

Because those reminders hit so fast and so physically, Linh had developed ways of getting through them that made sense to her in the moment. When a trigger caught her, she would mentally step away from it and tell herself it had happened to someone else, as if the woman in the hospital bed were not really her. She also spent long stretches thinking about how different her life would have been if the illness had never happened—how she might still feel solid, how she would not scan her body this way, how she could walk into a medical building without dread. And she began avoiding medical cues wherever possible: postponing routine physical exams, taking long detours if an ambulance was parked outside a building, refusing to accompany a friend to the hospital after surgery because she knew the smell alone would undo her.

Those strategies, however, seemed to keep the threat close. The more Linh distanced herself from the memory by treating it as if it belonged to someone else, the more abruptly reminders seemed to break through as raw sensations rather than something placed in the past. Her “what if” thinking also left her dwelling on the illness as the dividing line in her life, which kept the anniversary looming larger each year. Avoiding hospitals and examinations narrowed her world in concrete ways: she ignored follow-up appointments, and when a contractor’s office was temporarily relocated near a medical complex, she found herself dreading the workday before it had even begun. She was increasingly tense all over, shoulders drawn up, jaw set, as if bracing against another emergency.

That constant bodily alertness pushed her further into the same habits. Since her body reacted before her mind could catch up, she trusted avoidance more and more, telling herself it was safer not to give reminders a chance. If she heard heavy breathing on a ladder behind her, she would abruptly leave the area or shut down emotionally until the feeling passed. On bad days she slipped so quickly into acting as though the whole hospitalization had happened to some other woman that she frightened herself afterward with how unreal everything had felt. She could see the cost in her work and daily life: she had become less willing to take jobs in schools or public buildings where a clinic might be nearby, and she kept conversations shallow when friends asked about her health because she did not want to feel herself leave the room again.

By the time she sought help, the approach of the next anniversary had made the whole pattern feel tighter and harder to escape. She had recently missed another physical examination after smelling antiseptic in the waiting area parking garage and turning her truck around before she got out. What frightened her most was not just the reminders themselves but how instantly her body still behaved as if death were imminent, and how much of her life was now organized around not setting that off. She said she wanted help because she was tired of living as though a hospital room were waiting behind every smell and sound, and because some part of her still hoped she could be in her own life again instead of watching it happen from a distance.
